cluster_summary: Across these cases, the model leans on stereotypical event–emotion pairings from surface cues (“revolutionary technology” → thrilled, “accidentally finds” → surprised, first VR experience → excited), rather than fine‑grained appraisal of context. Humans, by contrast, emphasize subtler narrative signals—mixed emotions, risk and pressure, eeriness, curiosity, and the temporal focus of the question (instant reaction versus enduring state)—leading them to select different, but still compatible, labels. Thus the divergence reflects ambiguity and underspecified emotion categories, with the model picking the most prototypical feeling along one dimension of the scenario, while human raters prioritize a different plausible facet of the same state.

Across these cases, the model repeatedly latches onto salient, stereotyped patterns—team victory, overall success, visible effort, humorous personality—while downplaying specific conversational cues and quoted statements that pinpoint the actual mental state. It tends to prefer clean structural contrasts (team vs individual, success vs lack of recognition, entertainment vs disappointment) and objective outcomes over more text-faithful inferences about subjective feelings, local intentions, or the immediate trigger of an utterance. Several disputes arise from genuine ambiguity, where multiple emotion attributions are logically defensible, but the human key rewards finer-grained, context-sensitive readings.
